paper_metadata.title: An 8Gb/s 0.65mW/Gb/s Forwarded-Clock Receiver Using an ILO with Dual Feedback Loop and Quadrature Injection Scheme Ji-Hwan Seol1, Young-Ju Kim1, Sang-Hye Chung1, Kyoung-Soo Ha2, Seung-Jun Bae2, Jung-Bae Lee2, Joo Sun Choi2, Lee-Sup Kim1

figures.label: Fig. 23
figures.caption: Figure 23.6.1 shows a block diagram of our receiver. It consists of the ILO and data samplers. 1:4 demultiplexing is used to alleviate the operating speed of the ILO and data samplers. The ILO generates quadrature clocks for the data samplers and performs deskew. The ILO is composed of a main ILO, input mixer and quadrature injector, which are made of identical delay cells. The main ILO is a 2stage ring oscillator with an injection port at each delay cell. The injection clock for the main ILO’s first delay cell comes from the input mixer, which is used to reduce the required frequency tuning range for deskew. The input mixer also provides the input clock for the quadrature injector. The output clock of the quadrature injector is injected to the second delay cell of the main ILO for the generation of accurate multiphase clocks.

references.sentence: Figure 23.6.1 shows a block diagram of our receiver.

Figure 23.6.2 shows the block diagram of the main ILO and delay cell, which are drawn in the single ended style for the simplicity. 0° clock is fed back to the input A of the first delay cell to form an oscillation loop, and CKINJ is injected to the input B of the delay cell.
The principle of the dual feedback loop scheme of our ILO is shown in Fig. 23.6.3.
In this work, half delay line of the main oscillator is used for the generation of the quadrature injection clock as shown in Fig. 23.6.4.
Measured quadrature accuracy versus phase deskew curve is plotted in Fig. 23.6.4.
Figure 23.6.5 shows the measured JTB versus phase deskew of the ILO when the dual feedback loop scheme is on/off.
Jitter transfer and deskew curve is also shown in Fig. 23.6.5.
The comparison table of recent ILO-based forwarded-clock receivers is shown in Fig. 23.6.6.
The chip micrograph is shown in Fig. 23.6.7.
